items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.

items.title: Neurons don't 'fire harder' — they fire faster or not at all
items.claim: A neuron's action potential is all-or-nothing. The size of every action potential in a given neuron is essentially identical. Strong stimuli don't make bigger spikes — they make more spikes per second.

options.text: By the amplitude of each action potential
By the FREQUENCY of action potentials (and by the pattern of which neurons fire and when) — the rate code is the simplest model, but timing and synchrony also carry information
By the colour of the signal
By the chemical identity of each spike

items.reveal_title: Edgar Adrian and the discovery of the rate code
items.reveal:
Edgar Adrian (Nobel 1932) recorded from single sensory neurons in frogs and found: stretch a muscle and the neuron fires more spikes per second. Spike amplitude didn't change. The signal was the frequency.

Action potentials are regenerative — voltage-gated sodium channels self-amplify any membrane depolarisation past threshold into a stereotyped spike, then sodium channels inactivate and potassium channels repolarise. Sub-threshold stimuli produce no spike at all; supra-threshold stimuli produce one spike, of fixed size.

The brain reads intensity from spike rate, fine timing from spike intervals, and 'identity' from which neurons fired. Some neural systems (auditory, visual) encode information in spike timing to within a millisecond.
items.why: Sensory intensity feels continuous. The neuron encoding it is digital — and the continuous sensation is reconstructed from spike statistics.

items.title: Bread, beer and yoghurt all use the same biochemical loophole
items.claim: Without oxygen, glycolysis stops because cells run out of NAD+. Yeasts solve this by reducing pyruvate to ethanol (and releasing CO2). Muscles and lactic acid bacteria solve it by reducing pyruvate to lactate. Different products, same problem.

options.text: Both make ATP from the products
Both regenerate NAD+ from NADH so glycolysis can continue producing ATP (2 per glucose); the pyruvate must be 'dealt with' chemically because no oxygen is available to oxidise it via the Krebs cycle

items.reveal_title: NAD+ regeneration as the key step
items.reveal:
Glycolysis converts glucose to 2 pyruvate, producing 2 ATP and 2 NADH (reduced electron carrier). For glycolysis to continue running, NAD+ must be regenerated.

Aerobic cells: pyruvate enters mitochondria; Krebs cycle and electron transport oxidise NADH back to NAD+; oxygen is the final electron acceptor.

Anaerobic conditions: no oxygen, so no electron transport. Cells use pyruvate as the electron acceptor instead, dumping electrons from NADH onto it.

Yeasts (alcoholic fermentation): pyruvate -> acetaldehyde (releasing CO2) -> ethanol (using NADH, regenerating NAD+). Result: 2 ATP per glucose, plus ethanol and CO2. Bread rises from the CO2; beer accumulates ethanol.

Muscle and lactic acid bacteria (lactic fermentation): pyruvate -> lactate (using NADH, regenerating NAD+). Result: 2 ATP per glucose, plus lactic acid. Soured milk -> yoghurt; cabbage -> sauerkraut.

Aerobic respiration is about 15x more efficient (30-32 ATP vs 2). Fermentation is faster and works without oxygen. Both have their place.

Some organisms (facultative anaerobes like E. coli) switch between the two. Strict aerobes (most animals) die without oxygen within minutes. Strict anaerobes (Clostridium) die WITH oxygen — for them, O2 is toxic.
items.why: Bread, beer, wine, yoghurt and sauerkraut all rely on the same chemical trick to regenerate NAD+. Human civilisation has built food traditions on top of microbial anaerobic biochemistry.
